text:
Given your task update

T_i=Q_iQ_i^\top(W+R_i),

the top-r SVD components can be obtained efficiently from the smaller projected matrix

B_i=Q_i^\top(W+R_i).

Compute

B_i=\widehat U_i\Sigma_iV_i^\top.

Then

T_i=(Q_i\widehat U_i)\Sigma_iV_i^\top.

Define

U_i=Q_i\widehat U_i.

The rank-r truncated SVD is therefore

T_i^{(r)}
=
U_i^{(r)}S_i^{(r)}V_i^{(r)\top},

where U_i^{(r)}, S_i^{(r)}, and V_i^{(r)} correspond to the r largest singular values.

Concatenating components from all tasks

For N tasks, we concatenates the retained components:

U=
\left[
U_1^{(r)}
\mid
U_2^{(r)}
\mid
\cdots
\mid
U_N^{(r)}
\right]
\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times Nr},

V=
\left[
V_1^{(r)}
\mid
V_2^{(r)}
\mid
\cdots
\mid
V_N^{(r)}
\right]
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times Nr},

and constructs the block-diagonal singular-value matrix

S=
\operatorname{diag}
\left(
S_1^{(r)},S_2^{(r)},\ldots,S_N^{(r)}
\right)
\in\mathbb{R}^{Nr\times Nr}.

Before whitening, the direct concatenated reconstruction would be

T_{\text{concat}}=USV^\top.

However, although each U_i^{(r)} and V_i^{(r)} is orthonormal within its own task, the concatenated matrices generally do not satisfy

U^\top U=I,
\qquad
V^\top V=I.

For example, components from tasks i and j may overlap:

U_i^{(r)\top}U_j^{(r)}\neq 0,
\qquad
V_i^{(r)\top}V_j^{(r)}\neq 0.

This cross-task non-orthogonality is the conflict that whitening attempts to reduce.

Whitening the concatenated subspaces

S²MoE performs an SVD of each concatenated basis:

U=P_UD_UQ_U^\top,

V=P_VD_VQ_V^\top.

It then removes the singular-value scaling and constructs orthonormalized matrices:

U^\perp=P_UQ_U^\top,
\qquad
V^\perp=P_VQ_V^\top.

These are the polar factors of U and V. Assuming full column rank, they can equivalently be written as

U^\perp=U(U^\top U)^{-1/2},

V^\perp=V(V^\top V)^{-1/2}.

They satisfy

U^{\perp\top}U^\perp=I,
\qquad
V^{\perp\top}V^\perp=I.

The final merged task update is

\boxed{
T_{\text{merged}}
=
U^\perp S V^{\perp\top}
}

and the shared model weight becomes

\boxed{
\Theta_s
=
\Theta_{\mathrm{pre}}
+
T_{\text{merged}}.
}

This is the shared-module construction described in S²MoE.  

Substituting your projected task updates

Since

U_i^{(r)}
=
Q_i\widehat U_i^{(r)},

the concatenated left matrix is

U=
\left[
Q_1\widehat U_1^{(r)}
\mid
Q_2\widehat U_2^{(r)}
\mid
\cdots
\mid
Q_N\widehat U_N^{(r)}
\right].

Thus, in your setting,

T_{\text{merged}}
=
\operatorname{Polar}
\left(
[Q_1\widehat U_1^{(r)}|\cdots|Q_N\widehat U_N^{(r)}]
\right)
S
\operatorname{Polar}
\left(
[V_1^{(r)}|\cdots|V_N^{(r)}]
\right)^\top.

A key detail is that whitening is applied after concatenating all task subspaces, not independently to each task. Each task’s SVD vectors are already orthonormal internally; whitening is needed primarily to resolve overlap across different tasks.

Also, after whitening,

U^\perp S V^{\perp\top}

is generally not equal to the simple sum

\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i^{(r)}.

Whitening changes the singular directions to produce jointly orthogonal left and right bases while retaining the collected singular-value matrix S.

To construct the sparse experts in S²MoE, start from each fine-tuned model and subtract the shared model.

Let

\Theta_i

be the parameters of the model fine-tuned on task i, and let

\Theta_s
=
\Theta_{\text{pre}}+T_{\text{merged}}

be the shared model constructed from the merged low-rank components.

Then the residual expert for task i is

E_i=\Theta_i-\Theta_s.

This residual contains the task-specific information that is not already represented by the shared model.

1. Express the residual expert

Since

\Theta_i=\Theta_{\text{pre}}+T_i,

we have

E_i
=
\Theta_i-\Theta_s
=
T_i-T_{\text{merged}}.

For your projected task update,

T_i=Q_iQ_i^\top(W+R_i),

the expert residual becomes

\boxed{
E_i
=
Q_iQ_i^\top(W+R_i)-T_{\text{merged}}
}

for each layer or weight matrix.

This is the dense expert before pruning.

2. Apply magnitude pruning

Suppose a layer residual is

E_i\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.

Flatten it into a vector:

e_i=\operatorname{vec}(E_i).

Choose a retention ratio \rho\in[0,1]. If the layer has mn entries, retain

k=\lfloor \rho mn\rfloor

entries with the largest absolute values.

Define the index set

\mathcal I_i
=
\operatorname{TopKIndices}
\left(
|e_i|,k
\right).

The sparse expert is

\tilde e_{i,j}
=
\begin{cases}
e_{i,j}, & j\in\mathcal I_i,\\
0, & j\notin\mathcal I_i.
\end{cases}

After reshaping,

\boxed{
\tilde E_i
=
\operatorname{reshape}(\tilde e_i,m,n)
}

is the sparse expert for that layer.

Equivalently, using a binary mask M_i,

M_{i,j}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & |E_{i,j}|\text{ is among the top }k,\\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}

so that

\boxed{
\tilde E_i=M_i\odot E_i.
}

Here, \odot denotes elementwise multiplication.

3. Why top-magnitude pruning is used

The sparse approximation solves

\min_{\|\tilde E_i\|_0\leq k}
\|E_i-\tilde E_i\|_F^2.

Under a strict k-nonzero constraint, the optimal solution is to keep the k entries with the largest magnitudes.

Indeed, pruning an entry E_{i,j} contributes

E_{i,j}^2

to the reconstruction error. Therefore, the error is minimized by pruning the smallest-magnitude entries and retaining the largest ones.

This is exactly the sparse-expert construction used in the paper.  

4. Layer-wise construction

For a Transformer model, repeat the procedure for every prunable matrix:

E_i^{(\ell)}
=
\Theta_i^{(\ell)}
-
\Theta_s^{(\ell)}.

Then prune each matrix independently:

\tilde E_i^{(\ell)}
=
\operatorname{TopMagnitudePrune}
\left(
E_i^{(\ell)},\rho
\right).

The complete sparse expert is

\tilde\theta_i
=
\left\{
\tilde E_i^{(1)},
\tilde E_i^{(2)},
\ldots,
\tilde E_i^{(L)}
\right\}.

Typically, these can include attention projection matrices and feed-forward matrices. Biases, normalization parameters, or embeddings may be left unpruned depending on the implementation.

5. Final S²MoE layer computation

At inference, the shared output is

y_s^{(\ell)}
=
\Theta_s^{(\ell)}x^{(\ell)}.

The router selects sparse experts and computes

y_{\text{expert}}^{(\ell)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\tilde\alpha_i^{(\ell)}
\tilde E_i^{(\ell)}x^{(\ell)}.

The final layer output is

\boxed{
y^{(\ell)}
=
\Theta_s^{(\ell)}x^{(\ell)}
+
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\tilde\alpha_i^{(\ell)}
\tilde E_i^{(\ell)}x^{(\ell)}.
}

Thus, the effective weight for an input is

\Theta_{\text{effective}}^{(\ell)}(x)
=
\Theta_s^{(\ell)}
+
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\tilde\alpha_i^{(\ell)}
\tilde E_i^{(\ell)}.

Compact construction

For each task i,

\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
E_i
&=
\Theta_i-\Theta_s,\\
M_i
&=
\operatorname{TopKMask}(|E_i|,k),\\
\tilde E_i
&=
M_i\odot E_i.
\end{aligned}
}

One notation warning: in the paper, the sparsity parameter is sometimes described ambiguously. A “retention ratio of 0.2” means keeping 20% of the parameters and pruning 80%. Always state clearly whether \rho denotes the retained fraction or the pruned fraction.

Given: Two tasks, indexed by t∈{1,2}., One representative Transformer weight layer with pretrained weight matrix W₀∈ℝ^{2×2}., Task updates Δ₁=[[2,0],[0,0]] and Δ₂=[[0,0],[0,3]] used only as an illustrative example., Projected SVD rank r=1 for each task., Retained-entry fraction ρ∈[0,1], where ρ denotes the fraction retained and 1−ρ denotes the pruned fraction., A router produces task weights g₁(x),g₂(x), typically satisfying g₁(x)+g₂(x)=1 and g_t(x)≥0., A shared update is formed from the jointly whitened task subspace; sparse experts store pruned task-specific residuals.
Find: The construction of the shared low-rank module, the sparse task-specific experts, and the router-weighted inference rule.

1. Represent task adaptation as a weight update
   Wt=W₀+Δt, t∈\1,2\
   For each task, the adapted layer differs from the pretrained layer by an update matrix Δ_t. The construction operates on these updates rather than duplicating the entire pretrained matrix W₀.

2. Instantiate two small illustrative task updates
   Δ₁=begin bmatrix2&0\\0&0end bmatrix, Δ₂=begin bmatrix0&0\\0&3end bmatrix
   Task 1 changes the first coordinate direction, while task 2 changes the second coordinate direction. The matrices are deliberately diagonal so that their dominant singular directions remain visually readable.

3. Project each task update onto a rank-r SVD component
   Δt≈Δt⁽r⁾=Ut⁽r⁾Σt⁽r⁾bigl (Vt⁽r⁾bigr )^→p, r=1
   The rank-one truncated SVD retains only the largest singular value and its associated left and right singular vectors. This replaces a full task update by a low-rank component while preserving its dominant variation.

4. Read the rank-one SVDs in the concrete example
   Δ₁=2begin bmatrix1\\0end bmatrixbegin bmatrix1&0end bmatrix, Δ₂=3begin bmatrix0\\1end bmatrixbegin bmatrix0&1end bmatrix
   For this diagonal example, each update is already rank one. Task 1 has singular value 2 with left and right singular vectors aligned to the first coordinate; task 2 has singular value 3 with both vectors aligned to the second coordinate.

5. Package each retained SVD component as a parameter-space vector
   qt,₁=vec (Ut⁽¹⁾Σt⁽¹⁾bigl (Vt⁽¹⁾bigr )^→p ), qt,₁∈ℝ⁴
   Vectorization converts every retained matrix component into a vector in the same parameter space. This allows components from different tasks to be concatenated and orthonormalized jointly.

6. Concatenate all task subspaces before whitening
   Q=begin bmatrixq₁,₁&q₂,₁end bmatrix∈ℝ⁴×²
   The columns of Q contain the retained components from both tasks. Whitening is deliberately applied to this combined matrix, rather than separately whitening each task, so cross-task overlap and relative geometry are handled in one operation.

7. Compute the cross-task Gram matrix
   G=Q^→p Q
   The Gram matrix records norms on its diagonal and cross-task inner products off the diagonal. It is the matrix whose inverse square root removes scale and correlation from the concatenated components.

8. Apply polar-factor whitening
   Z=Q G⁻¹/²=Qbigl (Q^→p Qbigr )⁻¹/²
   The matrix Z contains jointly whitened basis vectors. The symmetric inverse square root rescales and decorrelates all task components simultaneously, producing the orthonormal factor associated with the polar decomposition of Q.

9. Verify orthonormality of the whitened basis
   Z^→p Z=bigl (Q^→p Qbigr )⁻¹/²Q^→p Qbigl (Q^→p Qbigr )⁻¹/²=I
   The middle factor is G, and the two surrounding factors are G^{-1/2}. Their product is the identity on the retained nonzero subspace. This is the key numerical property needed before projecting task updates into shared coordinates.

10. Project each task update into the whitened coordinates
   ct=Z^→pvec(Δt), widehat δt=Zct
   The coefficient vector c_t gives the coordinates of task t in the jointly whitened basis. The reconstructed vector \widehat{\delta}_t is the projection of the task update onto the span of all retained cross-task components.

11. Define one shared module from the jointly represented task coordinates
   bar c=∑t=₁²πt ct, πtge 0, ∑t=₁²πt=1, Eshared=mat(Zbar c)
   A shared update is formed by averaging or otherwise aggregating the task coordinates in the common whitened basis. The weights π_t can be uniform, data-frequency weighted, or selected according to a training objective. mat reverses vec and returns the matrix-shaped shared module.

12. Separate task-specific residuals from the shared update
   Rt=Δt-Eshared
   The residual R_t contains the part of task t that is not represented by the shared module. These residuals are the inputs to sparse expert construction, so task-specific capacity is spent only where the shared module is insufficient.

13. Retain the top-magnitude residual entries
   Et=mathcal Pρ(Rt), |supp(Et) |= lceil ρ N rceil , N=numel(Rt)
   The pruning operator keeps the entries of R_t with the largest absolute magnitudes and sets the remaining entries to zero. Here ρ is the retained fraction of entries; therefore the pruned fraction is 1−ρ. For a 2×2 matrix and ρ=1/2, two of the four entries are retained.

14. Write the sparse-expert decomposition used at inference
   Wtcompressed=W₀+Eshared+Et
   Each task-specific compressed model uses the common pretrained weight W₀, the shared module, and one sparse expert. The expert stores only the pruned residual correction, while the shared module carries cross-task structure.

15. Use router weights to mix task experts
   W(x)=W₀+Eshared+∑t=₁²gt(x)Et
   At inference time, the router assigns input-dependent weights to the sparse experts. A hard router can select one expert, while a soft router forms a weighted mixture. The shared module is applied independently of the router because it represents common structure.

16. State the complete S²MoE construction compactly
   boxed W(x)=W₀+mat (Z∑t=₁²πt Z^→pvec(Δt) )+∑t=₁²gt(x) mathcal Pρ (Δt-mat (Z∑s=₁²πs Z^→pvec(Δs) ) ), Z=Q(Q^→p Q)⁻¹/²
   The final expression first forms the jointly whitened basis from all task SVD components, constructs one shared projected update, subtracts that update from each task update, prunes each residual by retaining the top ρ fraction of entries, and finally combines the sparse experts using router weights.

Answer: boxed W(x)=W₀+Eshared+∑t=₁²gt(x)Et, Eshared=mat(Zbar c), bar c=∑t=₁²πtZ^→pvec(Δt), Et=mathcal Pρ (Δt-Eshared ), Z=Q(Q^→p Q)⁻¹/²
The shared module is obtained by taking rank-r SVD components from both task updates, vectorizing and concatenating them into Q, jointly whitening them with the polar factor Z=Q(QᵀQ)^{-1/2}, and aggregating the resulting task coordinates. Each sparse expert is the top-magnitude-pruned residual after subtracting the shared module, with ρ denoting the retained fraction and 1−ρ the pruned fraction. Router-weighted inference then adds the shared module and the weighted sparse experts to the pretrained layer.

operations.title: From Base Weights to Updates
operations.caption: W_t=W_0+\Delta_t,\qquad t\in\{1,2\}
operations.narration: Each task starts from the same pretrained layer and adds its own update. We store those updates rather than duplicating the full weight matrix.

operations.title: Two Illustrative Tasks
operations.caption: \Delta_1=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \Delta_2=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}
operations.narration: Task 1 changes the first coordinate direction, while Task 2 changes the second. The tiny matrices make the later subspace operations easy to see.

operations.title: Keep the Dominant Mode
operations.caption: \Delta_t\approx\Delta_t^{(r)}=U_t^{(r)}\Sigma_t^{(r)}(V_t^{(r)})^\top,\qquad r=1
operations.narration: We retain only the largest singular mode of each task update. This rank-one approximation is the first compression step.

operations.title: The Two Rank-One Components
operations.caption: \Delta_1=2\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \Delta_2=3\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&1\end{bmatrix}
operations.narration: In this illustrative example, both updates are already rank one. Their left and right singular directions align with separate coordinate axes.

operations.title: Vectorize the Components
operations.caption: q_{t,1}=\operatorname{vec}\!\left(U_t^{(1)}\Sigma_t^{(1)}(V_t^{(1)})^\top\right),\qquad q_{t,1}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}
operations.narration: Vectorization places every retained component in the same four-dimensional parameter space, so task components can be compared directly.

operations.title: Concatenate Across Tasks
operations.caption: Q=\begin{bmatrix}q_{1,1}&q_{2,1}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times2}
operations.narration: The two task columns enter one combined matrix before whitening. This preserves the cross-task geometry for the joint operation.

operations.title: Measure Cross-Task Geometry
operations.caption: G=Q^\top Q
operations.narration: The Gram matrix records each component's scale on the diagonal and their inner products off the diagonal.

operations.title: Polar-Factor Whitening
operations.caption: Z=QG^{-1/2}=Q\bigl(Q^\top Q\bigr)^{-1/2}
operations.narration: We multiply the concatenated components by the inverse square root of their Gram matrix. This jointly rescales and decorrelates the task directions.

operations.title: Verify Orthonormality
operations.caption: Z^\top Z=\bigl(Q^\top Q\bigr)^{-1/2}Q^\top Q\bigl(Q^\top Q\bigr)^{-1/2}=I
operations.narration: Whitening succeeds when the columns have unit norm and zero mutual inner product. They now form a stable shared coordinate system.

operations.title: Project into Shared Coordinates
operations.caption: c_t=Z^\top\operatorname{vec}(\Delta_t),\qquad \widehat{\delta}_t=Zc_t
operations.narration: Each task update is projected into the shared whitened basis. Its coefficients are c_t, and Zc_t reconstructs the retained projection.

operations.title: Build the Shared Module
operations.caption: \bar c=\sum_{t=1}^{2}\pi_t c_t,\qquad \pi_t\ge0,\qquad \sum_{t=1}^{2}\pi_t=1,\qquad E_{\mathrm{shared}}=\operatorname{mat}(Z\bar c)
operations.narration: We average the task coordinates with nonnegative weights summing to one. Reshaping the result produces one shared update.

operations.title: Subtract the Shared Part
operations.caption: R_t=\Delta_t-E_{\mathrm{shared}}
operations.narration: Subtracting the same shared module from each update leaves the task-specific residuals. These residuals are the inputs to expert sparsification.

operations.title: Prune by Magnitude
operations.caption: E_t=\mathcal{P}_{\rho}(R_t),\qquad \left|\operatorname{supp}(E_t)\right|=\left\lceil\rho N\right\rceil,\qquad N=\operatorname{numel}(R_t)
operations.narration: The pruning operator keeps the largest residual magnitudes and zeros the rest. With rho equal to one half, two of four entries survive; rho is the retained fraction.

operations.title: Assemble a Compressed Expert
operations.caption: W_t^{\mathrm{compressed}}=W_0+E_{\mathrm{shared}}+E_t
operations.narration: A compressed task model combines the pretrained layer, the persistent shared module, and one sparse task expert.

operations.title: Route at Inference
operations.caption: W(x)=W_0+E_{\mathrm{shared}}+\sum_{t=1}^{2}g_t(x)E_t
operations.narration: At inference, the router assigns input-dependent weights to the sparse experts. The shared module is always active, while the experts are mixed according to the router.

operations.title: FINAL ANSWER
operations.caption: W(x)=W_0+E_{\mathrm{shared}}+\sum_{t=1}^{2}g_t(x)E_t,\qquad E_{\mathrm{shared}}=\operatorname{mat}(Z\bar c),\quad E_t=\mathcal{P}_{\rho}(\Delta_t-E_{\mathrm{shared}}),\quad Z=Q(Q^\top Q)^{-1/2}
operations.narration: Rank-one task components are concatenated and jointly whitened to form Z. Their aggregated coordinates create the shared module, pruned residuals create sparse experts, and routing combines everything with the pretrained layer.
